risks.basis: THIS FILE has a confirmed defect on record
risks.risk: api/sc-auth.js checked the ROLE CLAIM inside a session token and never re-checked current credential state, so a deactivated admin kept acting for the remaining life of a 12h token -- removing other people and walking the licence toward the lockout the feature exists to prevent. CRITICAL under the defined vocabulary: after deactivation the caller is unauthorised, the access is destructive, and it was reachable on the real deployment rather than in principle

risks.basis: the same app (sairncode) has this defect on record
risks.risk: api/sc-credentials.js treated a 2xx whose representation body could not be parsed as a SUCCESSFUL write. Under Prefer: return=representation a PATCH that matched zero rows returns 200 with [], and the handler asked only whether the result was an array of length zero -- so .json().catch(() => null) turned an unreadable body into null, which is not an array, which is not length zero, and fell through to res.json({ok:true}). Driven on both write paths with the stored blob untouched: the main path returned 200 {ok:true} and the retry path 200 {ok:true, retried:true}, each over a write that did not happen, on a Tier A service-credential store whose own suite exists to refuse exactly that sentence

risks.basis: the same app (sairncode) has this defect on record
risks.risk: api/sd-data.js checkEnvelope built its BAD_ACTION message as action must be read or write, plus the word delete whenever isSc(resource) was true. isSc covers all 28 sc_ resources, but item 97 had split them into seven Tier A records granted only soft_delete and 21 granted delete. So a caller sending a bad action on a Tier A medical-billing record such as sc_claims was told the allowed verb is delete -- the exact verb the registry no longer grants there and which now answers 403 SOFT_DELETE_ONLY. Item 97 own reasoning is that a caller copying a working delete call from sc_dme to sc_claims should get a refusal naming the right verb; this message named the wrong one, unprompted, on the seven records that must never be destroyed. A test arm was asserting that wrong message on sc_denial, which is why it survived review.

risks.basis: the same app (sairncode) has this defect on record
risks.risk: SAIRNcode's Tier A write gate and soft-delete list both derive from one array in api/_resources/sairncode.js, and that array still held the seven names it was given on 2026-09-15 while docs/CRITICALITY-TIERS.md had grown to 23 Tier A sc_* rows. For eight days the sixteen in between accepted a write carrying the LICENCE KEY ALONE -- no employee session -- and could be hard-deleted: sc_anesthesia, sc_anesthesia_base_units, sc_auth, sc_auth_requests, sc_coded_items, sc_dme, sc_drg, sc_eligibility, sc_fraud, sc_hcc, sc_prebill, sc_providers, sc_query, sc_rac, sc_settings, sc_telehealth. Three of them are the reason this is critical rather than bookkeeping: sc_hcc is a named patient joined to a diagnosis grouping and its dollar value, sc_eligibility is a named patient joined to payer and plan, and sc_providers carries the QP status that selects between two CMS CY2026 conversion factors -- so a caller holding the licence string the app documents as NOT being auth could change what every unit billed under that provider is worth. The derivation was correct and the thing it derived from was stale, which is why every downstream gate was wrong at once.

risks.basis: the same app (sairncode) has this defect on record
risks.risk: scValidatePtSession's RTM GP warn keyed its family on the day-window maps (SC_RTM_SHORT/LONG_WINDOW), which disagree with CMS's sometimes-therapy designation in BOTH directions: 98978 and 98986 (the CBT device codes) sit in the window maps and are NOT CMS-designated -- the shipped warn told a coder CMS designated a code CMS never designated -- while 98975 (setup) and 98979/98980/98981 (treatment management) carry the designation with no day window and produced no warn at all. Found while discharging the review obligation on the warn, whose author's own attack point 2 asked exactly this question; answered by reaching the primary source (CMS MLN Matters MM14250 / CR 14250, which enumerates the family and the GP/GO/GN requirement verbatim) rather than by preference. The unpinned citation the warn shipped with -- disclosed honestly at the time -- is pinned against that document in the same fix.

risks.basis: the same app (sairncode) has this defect on record
risks.risk: SAIRNcode's Physical Therapy panel had no GP rule and no GP field: the word did not appear anywhere in sairncode.html. The panel checked the 8-minute rule, the KX threshold, CQ, MPPR and the 2026 RTM windows, and every one of those was correct -- but GP is the therapy DISCIPLINE modifier, required on every always-therapy service furnished under a physical-therapy plan of care (GO for occupational therapy, GN for speech-language pathology). A therapy line submitted without one is returned as UNPROCESSABLE: the claim is not denied, it is never adjudicated at all. So the panel's headline answer on a PT session with no GP was "No blocking issues found by the checks that ran" -- literally true, and the worst practically available answer, because the missing modifier was the one that stops the submission rather than one that changes what it pays. CQ costs 15%; KX costs an appeal; this costs the whole claim.

risks.basis: the same app (sairncode) has this defect on record
risks.risk: sairncode.html's PT validator was SILENT on an RTM line with no discipline modifier. The silence was deliberate and disclosed -- the GP rule's author wrote 'whether a therapist-furnished RTM service takes a discipline modifier was not verified' and asserted the silence in an arm -- but the question has an answer in the direction the silence did not cover: CMS designated the RTM code family SOMETIMES THERAPY in the CY2022 PFS final rule, and a sometimes-therapy service furnished under a therapy plan of care carries the discipline modifier (GP/GO/GN) like any always-therapy service. Everything in this panel is a PT plan-of-care context by construction -- the same scoping argument the GP rule itself makes for timed_minutes_by_code -- so an RTM line entered here takes GP on CMS's own framing, and the panel said nothing. Found by the independent review of cc's GP obligation and fixed as a WARN, not a block, at exactly the confidence the finding was stated at: the CY2022 rule is cited from review knowledge, NOT re-verified against a primary source in-session, and the gp_rtm source entry says so in its own text so the confidence travels with every rendered finding. The vm drive also caught a scope hazard before it shipped: the first draft reused the window section's `rtm` variable, declared BELOW the insertion point -- var hoisting would have thrown on the first RTM-carrying session.

risks.basis: the same app (sairncode) has this defect on record
risks.risk: tools/sc_tier_a_write_gate_live_probe.py -- the ONLY tool that checks SAIRNcode's Tier A write gate against the DEPLOYED function -- could not pass against a correct deployment, and one of its two broken arms would have failed by accusing the fix of being over-broad. Section 4 asserts a coder write is 403 FORBIDDEN on every name in `SIX`, which is DERIVED from api/_resources/sairncode.js -- so sc_coded_items joined that deny loop automatically when 5c781b99 re-tiered it A, while the same commit added `sc_coded_items: ['admin','biller','coder']` to SC_TIER_A_WRITE_ROLES_BY_RESOURCE precisely so coders kept their own panel. The probe's own CONTROL arm twelve lines later demands 200 on that identical call. Section 5b asserts `admin hard-delete on sc_coded_items still works -> 200` with failure text "the refusal is blanket rather than Tier A only", on a resource whose destroying `delete` verb the registry had just withdrawn. Both DRIVEN against the real handler in-process 2026-09-25: coder write -> 200 (probe expected 403), admin delete -> 400 (probe expected 200). A DERIVED LIST IS NOT AUTOMATICALLY A CORRECT LIST: the derivation was the right fix for the 2026-09-15 hand-written-six defect and is still right, but a derivation cannot know that a SECOND mechanism carves an exception out of the same population. Fixed by reading both sides from the handler -- a new write_role_overrides() parses the override map out of api/sd-data.js, the deny population is SIX minus the coder overrides, the coder-allowed names are driven as ALLOW, section 5's auditor loop (which excluded sc_compliance BY NAME, the same assumption one arm over) is derived the same way, and 5b's control moved onto RESOURCES-minus-Tier-A with UNVERIFIED rather than a pass if that population ever empties.

risks.basis: the same app (sairncode) has this defect on record
risks.risk: tests/sairncode_gates.js's WRITE_GATED table declares, one resource at a time, who may write each write-gated SAIRNcode resource -- and its own header says in capitals that it is THE CLAIM, the handler is THE FACT, and "a disagreement is a finding", spelled out by hand rather than generated precisely so it cannot agree with itself by construction. HALF OF IT WAS NEVER READ. The only consumer anywhere in the suite was `Object.keys(WRITE_GATED)`, so the resource-name half was compared against the handler and the ROLE half ('admin|biller' etc) was decoration. It had already drifted: `sc_coded_items: 'admin|biller'` while the handler granted ['admin','biller','coder'], from 5c781b99 on 2026-09-23 until 2026-09-25. Every OTHER role assertion in the suite goes through rolesFor(), which PARSES SC_TIER_A_WRITE_ROLES, SC_TIER_A_WRITE_ROLES_BY_RESOURCE and sc_settings' narrowing out of api/sd-data.js -- correct for catching a gate that disappears, and structurally incapable of catching one that is WIDENED, because it derives from the thing being widened. So the one independent hand-written statement of who may write what was the one thing nothing read. Fixed: the cell is corrected and a new arm compares the table's role half against rolesFor() for all 24 rows. DRIVEN NEGATIVE IN BOTH DIRECTIONS in a throwaway git worktree, never in the clone -- restoring the old 'admin|biller' cell fails the arm and names the disagreeing row, and ADDING 'auditor' to the handler's sc_coded_items override fails it too and fails it FIRST, i.e. it is the discriminating arm. Also corrected: the comment `// the one per-resource override`, which has described two overrides since 2026-09-23.

risks.basis: the same app (sairncode) has this defect on record
risks.risk: api/sd-data.js argued a live authorization decision from a premise that had stopped being true, in two places, one of them inside the override map's own header. The paragraph "TWO THINGS TO DECIDE AGAINST REAL USE" said "the coder's own resource is sc_coded_items, which is NOT gated, so the split is coherent", and the sc_claims entry in SC_TIER_A_WRITE_ROLES_BY_RESOURCE's header said "sc_coded_items, is ungated and that is their real job" -- both the stated GROUNDS for excluding `coder` from sc_claims. 5c781b99 re-tiered sc_coded_items A on 2026-09-23 because the row carries a verbatim quote from a clinical note, so it has required a real employee session since then. The CONCLUSION still holds and the REASON does not: what keeps coders on their own resource is now a named exception in that same map, which is a stronger footing than an absent gate but not the same one. The same "UNGATED" wording was in tools/sc_tier_a_write_gate_live_probe.py's docstring, where it sat directly above the two arms that had gone self-contradictory for exactly this reason. Not cosmetic: the next session asked to widen or narrow sc_claims reads that paragraph, and it argues from a fact about the codebase that is false. Corrected in all three places, with the old wording and its date kept rather than deleted, so a reader can see the argument moved rather than finding a clean comment that was never wrong.

risks.basis: the same app (sairncode) has this defect on record
risks.risk: sairncode.html, TWO sites, both free-text inputs interpolated into a SYSTEM prompt raw. (1) The 2026 code-lookup prompt took #code-lookup-desc -- an <input type=text> whose placeholder invites a sentence ("established patient office visit, moderate complexity") -- and the described procedure reached the model inside the instruction block of a prompt whose whole job is to refuse fabrication ("never invent a plausible-sounding code number ... set no_match:true"). (2) The NCCI claim-scrub prompt embedded #scrub-code1 and #scrub-code2 MID-SENTENCE: 'whether CPT/HCPCS/ICD-10 codes "' + code1 + '" and "' + code2 + '" have a known ... edit conflict'. Both outputs drive billing decisions -- a steered answer is a coding recommendation a biller acts on. FIXED by routing all three fields through sfFence/sfRule, the byte-identical client mirror of api/_lib/prompt-fence.js. The claim-scrub sentence was rewritten to refer to the codes at the end of the prompt rather than embed them, because a fence in the middle of a sentence is not a fence -- the block has to be a block. Nothing is filtered; all three still reach the model, labelled as data, with both fence markers mechanically defanged. THE SCANNER STILL CANNOT SEE THE CLAIM-SCRUB SITE AT ALL: code1/code2 are app-specific names no generic word list can carry, which is the per-app field list that remains unwritten. `desc` was added to the word list; the code fields were found only by reading.

risks.basis: the same app (sairncode) has this defect on record
risks.risk: THE CIPHERTEXT CENSUS READ A JSON PATH THAT IS ALWAYS NULL, AND ITS ZERO GATES A DESTRUCTIVE STEP. sql/legacy_ciphertext_census.sql and sql/sd_encryption_key_revoke_2026-09-24.sql:113 both read `sc_credentials.data->>'enc'`, which assumes the ciphertext is a top-level key. api/sc-credentials.js:200-205 writes `next[service] = { enc, last4, updated_at }`, so the real path is `data->'stedi'->>'enc'`. A wrong jsonb path returns NULL rather than erroring, so every count came back legacy_rows = 0, v2_rows = 0, never_set_rows = total_rows -- and legacy_rows = 0 IS the precondition step 4 of the revoke file waits for before clearing SD_AUTH_SECRET_PREVIOUS. The wrong path would have authorised clearing the old key while legacy ciphertext was still in the table, and the census is the document that would have authorised it. Found by fourth's b19 discharge as F1, on the one attack point of six that the 2026-09-29 review never examined. Fixed to walk jsonb_each(data) so a second service is counted the day it is written rather than the day somebody re-reads the file, and a new PART 0 counts the flat and nested shapes separately so both-zero reads as 'no credential exists' rather than as the step-4 precondition.
